Name: belief_state_velocity
Title: Belief-State Velocity: Measuring Internal Representational Movement to Prune Inert Reasoning Tokens
Short Hypothesis: The mechanistic signal for whether a chain-of-thought (CoT) token does useful work is not its output-distribution surprisal but how much it moves the model's internal answer-relevant belief state. We hypothesize a low-dimensional 'belief-state velocity'—the movement of the residual stream projected onto the subspace that encodes the eventual answer—sharply distinguishes load-bearing tokens (high velocity) from inert filler (near-zero velocity), enabling a training-free pruning/early-exit controller that outperforms surprisal-based methods (ASAP, CAID/PACE) at matched compression.
Related Work: Recent step-pruning methods use output-distribution signals: ASAP prunes via first-token surprisal, and CAID/PACE define 'context-aware information density' from token-level information theory over the output distribution. These are output-space quantities and can be fooled by tokens that are surprising yet answer-irrelevant, or fluent yet decisive. Heima compresses CoT into latent thinking tokens via retraining. My prior proposals target specific behaviors (load-bearing tokens via attention/ablation, answer commitment, recomputation, overthinking circuits, budget direction, branch precommitment). This proposal is distinct: it defines a single, cheap, training-free MECHANISTIC information-gain signal—movement of the residual stream within the answer-encoding subspace ('belief-state velocity')—computed from internal states rather than output logits, and shows it is a better inertness detector than surprisal because it measures effect on the internal answer belief rather than local next-token predictability.
Abstract: Long chain-of-thought (CoT) traces contain many tokens that add little to the eventual answer, but detecting them cheaply and reliably is hard. Existing training-free detectors rely on output-distribution signals such as first-token surprisal or context-aware information density; these measure local next-token predictability and can misclassify tokens that are surprising but answer-irrelevant, or fluent but decisive. We propose a mechanistic alternative: 'belief-state velocity,' the magnitude of movement of the residual stream projected onto a low-dimensional answer-encoding subspace between consecutive positions. Intuitively, a token does useful reasoning work only if it changes the model's internal estimate of the answer; inert filler leaves the belief state nearly stationary. We estimate the answer subspace once per model using a lightweight probe on final-position hidden states, then compute belief-state velocity online for free during generation. We first validate that low-velocity tokens can be causally ablated with far fewer answer flips than high-velocity tokens, and that velocity outperforms surprisal/CAID at ranking tokens by causal importance (AUC against ablation ground truth). We then build a training-free controller that (i) skips or compresses runs of low-velocity tokens and (ii) triggers early exit once belief-state velocity decays to near-zero for a sustained window (belief has converged). On GSM8K, MATH, and ProntoQA across DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B and Qwen2.5-7B, we compare accuracy-vs-tokens Pareto curves against ASAP-style surprisal pruning, CAID/PACE, fixed truncation, and full CoT, expecting 25-45% token savings at matched accuracy plus a mechanistic account of reasoning inertness.
Experiments: 1. Answer subspace estimation: For each model (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B, Qwen2.5-7B), train a lightweight linear probe on final-prompt/answer-position hidden states to predict the eventual answer (MCQ label for ProntoQA/ARC; numeric bucket / token for GSM8K/MATH). The probe's weight rows define a low-dimensional answer subspace; select the layer maximizing probe accuracy on held-out data. 2. Belief-state velocity signal: During full-CoT generation, at each token compute the projection of the residual stream onto the answer subspace and define velocity as the L2 norm of the difference between consecutive projected states (optionally normalized). Also compute output-based baselines: next-token entropy, first-token surprisal (ASAP), and CAID information density. 3. Causal validation: Sample tokens across the velocity distribution and mean-ablate each token's residual contribution, recording answer flips. Test that low-velocity tokens flip answers far less often; report answer-flip rate vs velocity bin and AUC of velocity vs surprisal/CAID at predicting the ablation ground truth. 4. Characterization: Report distribution of velocity across GSM8K/MATH/ProntoQA, correlation with difficulty and CoT length, and which token/phrase types are low-velocity (hedging, restating). 5. Pruning controller (training-free): Two modes—(a) skip/compress: suppress generation of runs where predicted velocity stays below a threshold (using a one-step-ahead velocity estimate or a tiny probe on current state); (b) convergence early-exit: force answer emission once velocity stays below threshold for W consecutive tokens. 6. Evaluation: accuracy vs mean tokens generated (Pareto) and wall-clock latency; baselines: full CoT, fixed truncation, entropy early-exit, ASAP-style surprisal pruning, CAID/PACE. Metrics: accuracy, tokens, velocity-vs-ablation AUC, fraction pruned. 7. Ablations: subspace dimensionality (top-k probe directions), layer choice, normalization, threshold/window sweeps, cross-dataset and cross-model transfer of the subspace, and velocity vs surprisal head-to-head at matched compression.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. The answer subspace estimated by a probe may be imperfect for open-ended math answers; we restrict to extractable numeric answers and validate with causal ablation rather than probe accuracy alone. 2. Velocity computed post-hoc is trivial, but the online skip mode requires a one-step-ahead estimate, which may be noisy; we test both a next-token-look-ahead variant and a tiny probe on the current state, and fall back to the convergence early-exit mode which needs no look-ahead. 3. Some low-velocity tokens may set up later high-velocity computation (verification), so aggressive pruning could hurt hard items—the Pareto and per-difficulty analyses quantify this. 4. Belief-state velocity may be more diffuse (less sparse) for some models, limiting savings; characterization quantifies this. 5. Subspace may not transfer across models/datasets, requiring cheap one-time per-model estimation; transfer is tested explicitly. 6. Velocity might correlate with surprisal, weakening the novelty claim; the head-to-head AUC and matched-compression comparison directly test whether the internal signal adds value over output-space signals.
